title: A School Blog and Geothermal Energy

listening1.context: You are going to hear a conversation between Maryam and Hamad.

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: Hi Hamad! Ms Fatma says we can start a school blog. Have you thought about what we should write?

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Yes, I have. I would like a blog about school sports, because everybody loves the football matches.

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: Sports is a good idea, but the teams already have a noticeboard. How about school trips? Students could read about each trip and look at the photos.

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Good idea. Many students miss the trips, so they will enjoy reading about them. Which website shall we use?

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: My brother uses one called Quick Notes, but it shows too many adverts. Mr Ahmed from the IT department suggests Bright Pages. It is free and safe.

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Then let's use Bright Pages. How often should we post? Once a week is easy, but readers might forget us.

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: Every day would be too much work for two students. What about two posts every week?

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Perfect, twice a week. Now, who is going to take the photos? I am not good at it.

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: I will take them. My uncle gave me a good camera. You can write the text, because your spelling is better than mine.

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Thanks. Should readers be able to leave comments under our posts?

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: Yes, but some comments might be rude. Ms Fatma will read every comment before it appears on the blog. Mr Ahmed will help us with the settings.

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Wonderful. When can we publish the first post? I am free on Sunday, but you have a club meeting that day.

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: That is right. Tuesday is library day, so let's choose Thursday. That gives us enough time to prepare.

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Thursday is fine. What shall we write about first? Last month's visit to the Science Centre, or last week's visit to the date farm?

script.speaker: Maryam
script.text: The Science Centre trip was a long time ago, and people have forgotten it. Let's write about the date farm. The photos are still fresh.

script.speaker: Hamad
script.text: Great. I will start writing tonight and send you the text tomorrow. I think our blog is going to be popular.

items.q: What will the blog be about?
Who will read the comments before they appear?
On which day will they publish the first post?
What will the first post be about?

listening2.context: You are going to hear a talk about geothermal energy.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Hello, everyone. Today I am going to talk about geothermal energy, which is heat that comes from deep inside the Earth.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: If you dig deep under the ground, it gets hotter and hotter. In some places, the rock under the surface is so hot that it turns underground water into steam. The word geothermal comes from two Greek words: geo, which means Earth, and therme, which means heat.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: People have used this heat for thousands of years. The ancient Romans built public baths that were warmed by hot springs. Electricity from geothermal steam was produced for the first time in Italy, in nineteen oh four.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: A geothermal power station works in a simple way. Workers drill a deep well into the hot rock. Steam rises up the well and turns a turbine. The turbine drives a generator, and the generator makes electricity. After that, the steam cools down and turns back into water, and the water is pumped under the ground again. That is why geothermal energy is renewable.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Iceland is famous for geothermal energy. The country sits on a place where two huge plates of the Earth's crust meet, so there is a lot of heat close to the surface. Geothermal energy heats most of the houses in Iceland, and it also gives the country about thirty percent of its electricity.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Geothermal energy has several advantages. A power station can work day and night, in sunny, windy or cloudy weather. It needs only a small piece of land, and it produces very little pollution.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: However, there are some problems. Geothermal energy can only be used in places where hot rock is close to the surface, so it is not possible in every country. Drilling deep wells is also very expensive.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: What about Oman? There are some natural hot springs here, for example Ain Al Kasfa near Nakhal, where people go to swim. But Oman has no big geothermal power stations, and it prefers to use the strong sun for solar energy instead.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Thank you for listening.

short.q: What does the Greek word 'therme' mean?
In which year was electricity first produced from geothermal steam?
What turns the turbine in a geothermal power station?
Which country uses geothermal energy to heat most of its houses?
